name: Avenida dos Aliados
short: Porto’s main avenue, laid out from 1916; granite Beaux-Arts buildings and a City Hall with a 70-metre tower.
long: Avenida dos Aliados is Porto’s “drawing room” and civic axis, linking Praça da Liberdade to Praça do General Humberto Delgado. It was laid out from 1 February 1916 on a plan by the English architect Barry Parker, sweeping away medieval lanes. Monumental granite Beaux-Arts buildings line the avenue, which is closed by the City Hall with its 70-metre tower and carillon clock.
history:
Work began on 1 February 1916 in the presence of President Bernardino Machado: the ceremony consisted of dismantling the “first stone” of the Baroque palace on Praça da Liberdade where the city council had sat since 1816. That same day the council approved the project for the new City Hall above the Aliados, part of a plan to expand the civic centre drawn up by the English architect Barry Parker. The avenue opened in 1917; it was first called Avenida das Nações Aliadas, after the Allied nations of the First World War, and is 250 metres long.

Before the avenue there was a maze of short streets and alleys known locally as “os lavadouros”, crossed by two busy parallel streets, Rua de D. Pedro and Rua do Laranjal. The avenue’s axis is marked by a broad central strip, gardened until mid-2006 and now fully paved in granite. When the gardens were removed, the entrances to the Congregados pedestrian tunnel were also sealed.

All the avenue’s buildings are of good granite, many crowned with dormers, domes and finials. They include the “A Nacional” insurance building by Marques da Silva, the former “O Comércio do Porto” newspaper building by Rogério de Azevedo, and the Caixa Geral de Depósitos with a large colonnade and a domed turret by Porfírio Pardal Monteiro. In the former Café Imperial, now a McDonald’s, one of the city’s finest interiors survives.

The City Hall (Paços do Concelho) followed Parker’s plan as revised by Correia da Silva: construction began in 1920, but the council services only moved in in 1957. The building has six floors, a basement and two inner courtyards, and its central tower, 70 metres high, carries a carillon clock; it was the last monumental granite palace built in Portugal.

In the middle of the avenue stands the statue “A Juventude” (“Youth”, also called “Menina dos Aliados”) by the sculptor Henrique Moreira, installed in 1929. Beneath the avenue runs the Aliados metro station on line D, whose remodelling was the subject of great debate; the redesign was by Álvaro Siza Vieira and Eduardo Souto de Moura. Two papal masses have been held on the Aliados: John Paul II on 15 May 1982 and Benedict XVI on 14 May 2010, attended by 120,000–150,000 people.
facts: Work began on 1 February 1916 in the presence of President Bernardino Machado.
The avenue is 250 metres long; its former name was Avenida das Nações Aliadas, after the Allies of the First World War.
The civic-centre expansion plan was drawn up by the English architect Barry Parker.
The City Hall was designed by Correia da Silva: construction began in 1920 and services moved in in 1957.
The central tower of the City Hall is 70 metres high, with a clock and carillon.
The central strip was gardened until 2006 and then fully paved in granite.
The statue “A Juventude”, by the sculptor Henrique Moreira, was installed in 1929.
tip: Start at Praça da Liberdade and walk up to the City Hall — that way the avenue unfolds in full. The Aliados metro station (line D) lies right under the central strip. Morning light falls on the western side, evening light on the City Hall. São Bento station and the Clérigos tower are close by.
